lessonTitle: Kinetics in Curvilinear Motion: Banking, Friction and Loops

blocks.text: Velodrome tracks are tilted so steeply that a cyclist leans into the bank at high speed and needs no sideways grip from the tyres at all. A motorway bend is built with a gentle tilt for the same reason. Newton's second law applied to circular motion tells us exactly how much tilt a given speed and radius demand.

blocks.markdown: In curvilinear motion the net force on a particle of mass $m$ (kg) has a component along the path and a component toward the centre of curvature. The towards-the-centre direction is called the **normal** direction, and Newton's second law reads $\sum F_n=ma_n=mv^2/\rho$ and $\sum F_t=ma_t=m\dot v$. The quantity $mv^2/\rho$ is not a new force: it is the required resultant of the real forces (gravity, normal reaction, friction, tension) pointing toward the centre.

blocks.title: No 'centrifugal force' needed
blocks.text: In an inertial frame there is no outward force on the particle. Whenever the particle moves on a curved path, the real forces must supply a net inward force $mv^2/\rho$. If they cannot, the particle does not follow the path: it skids or leaves the surface.

blocks.caption: Take the positive normal direction toward the centre of curvature, and $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$ wherever gravity enters.

blocks.markdown: **Banked curve without lateral friction.** A vehicle of mass $m$ rounds a circular bend of radius $\rho$ on a road banked at angle $\theta$ to the horizontal. If there is no sideways friction, only the road's normal reaction $N$ (perpendicular to the surface) and weight $mg$ act. Vertically the net force is zero, $N\cos\theta=mg$; horizontally toward the centre, $N\sin\theta=mv^2/\rho$. Dividing eliminates $N$ and $m$.

blocks.caption: Design banking angle: independent of mass.

blocks.title: Banking angle for a motorway bend
blocks.prompt: A bend of radius 150 m is to be banked so that vehicles at 25 m/s need no sideways friction. Find the banking angle.

steps.text: Resolve: vertical equilibrium and horizontal centripetal equation.

blocks.markdown: **Vertical loop.** On a vertical circular path the weight has a normal component that changes around the loop. At the bottom the centre is above the particle, so $N-mg=mv^2/r$; at the top the centre is below it, so $N+mg=mv^2/r$. The normal reaction is therefore largest at the bottom and smallest at the top, and a particle remains in contact only if $N\ge0$, giving the minimum speed at the top $v_{min}=\sqrt{gr}$.

blocks.title: Normal force on a rider in a loop
blocks.prompt: A rider of mass 60 kg travels on a vertical loop of radius 12 m. Find the normal force from the seat at the bottom with a speed of 20 m/s, and at the top with a speed of 12 m/s ($g=9.81$ m/s$^2$).

steps.text: Bottom: centre above, so $N$ up and weight down; net upward force is the centripetal force.
Top: centre below, so $N$ and weight both point toward the centre.
Check the minimum speed at the top.

blocks.answer: $N_b\approx2589$ N (about 4.4 times the rider's weight of 589 N) and $N_t\approx131$ N.

blocks.markdown: **Flat curve with friction.** On a level road the only horizontal force on a car is friction between the tyres and the road. For no slipping, the friction force needed is $F=mv^2/\rho$, and it cannot exceed its limiting value $\mu N=\mu mg$, where $\mu$ is the coefficient of static friction. The limiting condition gives the maximum speed.

blocks.caption: Independent of mass; increases with $\sqrt{\rho}$ and $\sqrt{\mu}$.

blocks.title: Maximum speed on a flat bend
blocks.prompt: A flat circular bend has radius 90 m and the tyre-road coefficient of static friction is $\mu=0.70$ (typical for dry asphalt). Find the greatest speed that avoids skidding.

steps.text: Limiting friction supplies the centripetal force.

blocks.answer: The maximum speed is about 24.9 m/s (roughly 90 km/h); a wet road with a lower $\mu$ lowers it.

blocks.title: Direction of the normal axis
blocks.text: Always take the positive normal direction toward the centre. At the top of a loop weight adds to the inward force; at the bottom it subtracts. A negative computed $N$ means the particle has left the surface and the circular-path assumption is invalid.

points: Newton's second law in path coordinates: $\sum F_n=mv^2/\rho$ toward the centre and $\sum F_t=m\dot v$ along the path.
Banking without friction: $\tan\theta=v^2/(g\rho)$; flat curve: $v_{max}=\sqrt{\mu g\rho}$; both are independent of the vehicle's mass.
Vertical loop: $N=m(g+v^2/r)$ at the bottom and $N=m(v^2/r-g)$ at the top, with minimum top speed $\sqrt{gr}$.

questions.stem: A road bend is banked for no-friction cornering at its design speed. Which of the following does NOT affect the required banking angle?

distractorRationale.d: Speed appears squared in the formula.

questions.explanation: Dividing the horizontal and vertical equations of motion cancels both $N$ and $m$, leaving $\tan\theta=v^2/(g\rho)$. A truck and a bicycle therefore need the same banking at the same speed and radius.

questions.stem: A car on a flat bend has a maximum non-skidding speed $v_{max}$. If the radius of the bend were four times larger, with the same road surface, the new maximum speed would be
questions.explanation: From $v_{max}=\sqrt{\mu g\rho}$, the speed varies with the square root of the radius. A four-fold radius therefore gives only a two-fold speed.

questions.stem: A car passes through the lowest point of a smooth dip in a road, travelling at constant speed along a circular arc. Compared with its weight $mg$, the normal force from the road is

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the net force must be upward, $N-mg=mv^2/r>0$.
distractorRationale.b: Equal only if the car is not on a curve.
distractorRationale.c: This is the situation on a crest, not in a dip.
distractorRationale.d: Zero would mean the car loses contact.

questions.explanation: At the bottom of a circular dip, the centre of curvature is above the car, so the net force must point upward. This requires $N=mg+mv^2/r$, which exceeds the weight.

questions.stem: A car-sized toy moves on the inside of a vertical circular track of radius 10 m. Taking $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$, the minimum speed at the top for contact to be maintained is approximately

distractorRationale.a: This is $\sqrt{gr}/2$, not a result of any equation.
distractorRationale.c: Confuses the value of $g$ with a speed.
distractorRationale.d: This is $\sqrt{2gr}$, which is not the contact condition.

questions.explanation: At the top, $N+mg=mv^2/r$, and contact is lost when $N=0$, so $v_{min}=\sqrt{gr}=\sqrt{9.81\times10}=9.9$ m/s. At lower speed the track can no longer supply the required inward force without pulling.

questions.stem: A vehicle travels around a frictionless banked curve at a speed above the design speed. For it to avoid sliding up the bank, the friction force from the road must

options.text: Act perpendicular to the road surface

distractorRationale.a: Zero friction is only possible at exactly the design speed.
distractorRationale.b: Perpendicular is the direction of the normal reaction, not friction.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: more inward force is needed than the horizontal part of $N$ gives, so friction must contribute down the slope.
distractorRationale.d: Up-slope friction reduces the inward force and would apply below the design speed.

questions.explanation: At the design speed the normal reaction alone provides the required centripetal force. At a higher speed more inward force is needed, so friction must act down the incline to supply the extra.

questions.stem: A flat bend has a radius of 50 m and a tyre-road static friction coefficient of 0.45. Taking $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$, find the maximum speed at which a car can take it without skidding, in m/s.
questions.explanation: At the limit, $\mu mg=mv^2/\rho$, so $v=\sqrt{\mu g\rho}=\sqrt{0.45\times9.81\times50}=14.9$ m/s. The mass cancels.

questions.stem: A railway curve of radius 40 m is to be banked so that a test trolley at 15 m/s needs no lateral wheel force. Taking $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$, find the banking angle in degrees.
questions.explanation: From $\tan\theta=v^2/(g\rho)=225/(9.81\times40)=0.5734$, the angle is $\theta=29.8^\circ$. The trolley's mass does not appear.

questions.stem: A pilot of mass 75 kg flies a vertical circle of radius 300 m. At the top of the loop (inverted) the speed is 90 m/s. Taking $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$, find the force exerted on the pilot by the seat, in newtons.
questions.explanation: At the top, the seat force and the weight both point toward the centre (downward), so $N+mg=mv^2/r$. Hence $N=75(8100/300-9.81)=75(27-9.81)=1289$ N.

questions.stem: Derive the banking angle $\tan\theta=v^2/(g\rho)$ for a frictionless banked curve. State the forces, the equations used and the assumptions made.
markingGuide: Forces: weight $mg$ downward and normal reaction $N$ perpendicular to the road surface (no friction).
Horizontal inward: $N\sin\theta=mv^2/\rho$ since the acceleration is toward the centre of the circle, horizontally.
Assumptions: circular path in a horizontal plane, constant speed, no lateral friction, vehicle treated as a particle.
questions.explanation: The only force with a horizontal component is the normal reaction, so its horizontal part supplies the centripetal force while its vertical part balances the weight. Their ratio gives the angle.

questions.stem: A car travels at constant speed round a flat bend. Explain, using Newton's second law in an inertial frame, why the car skids when it goes too fast, derive the maximum safe speed and discuss the effect of a wet road.
markingGuide: Required inward force is $mv^2/\rho$ and the only horizontal force is friction.
Friction is limited: $F\le\mu N=\mu mg$ on a level road.
If $v>v_{max}$ friction cannot provide the force, so the car continues more nearly straight (tangentially) and slides outward; no outward force is needed to explain this.
On a wet road $\mu$ is smaller so $v_{max}$ is smaller; mass has no effect.
questions.explanation: Skidding happens when the required centripetal force exceeds the available friction. The car's inertia keeps it moving along a straighter line, which looks like being thrown outward from the car's own frame.
